headline: Nvidia beat everything and the stock FELL first - $96.2B of revenue, +106%, and a Q3 guide of $108B against $104.2B expected, yet it took roughly 40 minutes and a 70% FY28 growth number on the call to turn it. Now +6-7% pre-market. Meanwhile hike odds ROSE at every meeting and crude fell a fifth day. Warsh speaks tomorrow at 10:00
client_frame_short:
The question this morning: "Nvidia crushed the numbers, so why did the stock go DOWN first?" It did, for about 40 minutes. Revenue was $96.2 billion, up 106% in a year, and next quarter's guide came in above what Wall Street wanted. The stock only turned higher once management put a 2028 growth number on the call. It is up 6-7% before the open. **The AI trade is now paying for next year's story rather than for the results already delivered.**

Nothing here needs a decision from you. Two things are worth knowing. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge held at 3.3% yesterday, a 65th straight month above target, and the odds of a rate HIKE by December rose again overnight to 73%. Chair Warsh gives his first Jackson Hole speech tomorrow at 10:00. Quietly helpful: oil fell a fifth day on Gulf diplomacy.
client_frame:
Start with what actually happened, because the headline and the tape disagreed for the better part of an hour. Nvidia reported revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year, with data-centre revenue of $89 billion, up 117%, and guided the current quarter to $108 billion plus or minus 2% against roughly $104.2 billion expected. Those figures are from the company's own release. And the stock went down. Reuters is the only source that reconciles the sequence: shares opened the after-hours session lower, were little changed for about 40 minutes, and the mood picked up with the conference call, after which Nvidia rose 4.2% on more than 50 million shares. What changed inside those 40 minutes was not a number from the quarter just ended - it was management putting roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028 on the call. By this morning the stock is quoted between $223.62 and $225.21, up 6.7% to 7.4% depending on the snapshot, and Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya's line captures the mood: no matter how high the expectations were, Nvidia managed to beat all of them.

The part I would actually raise with a client is the margin, not the revenue. Nvidia guided gross margin DOWN - 74.0% this quarter, troughing at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter, on rising memory costs. On the very same evening, HP Inc. beat revenue by $1.24 billion and fell roughly 9% overnight after its CFO flagged below-seasonal fourth-quarter revenue on commodity-driven price increases and rising memory costs. Two companies at opposite ends of the technology stack naming the identical cause. That is a hardware cost cycle turning, not a demand problem, and it is a more durable fact than any single quarter's revenue beat. The wider pattern from last night is worth naming plainly: of four large after-close reporters, three beat and two were sold. Salesforce rose about 11% and CrowdStrike about 9%, while Synopsys beat cleanly and fell 1.3% and HP beat enormously and was punished. The print is not the risk; the guide and the margin path are.

Now the uncomfortable half. While equities celebrated a forward narrative, the interest-rate market moved the other way, and it moved uniformly. Our own CME cohort refreshed to Wednesday's settle and cumulative hike odds ROSE at every single meeting - 39.6% for September, 54.3% by October, 73.5% by December and 78.2% by January - with the probability of a CUT still exactly zero at every meeting through January 2027. The cause was yesterday morning's data. Core PCE held at 3.3% year over year, which Reuters notes is the 65th consecutive month above the Fed's 2% target, and the unrounded monthly figure was 0.246%, a whisker below the rounding boundary. Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid put it best: while July core PCE came in line with consensus, the details of the release were more inflationary. Underneath a headline second-quarter GDP figure of just 1.5%, real final sales to private domestic purchasers ran at 4.2%, the strongest in over three years. Soft headline growth, hot private demand, sticky inflation, and a labour market near cycle lows on claims. Boston's Susan Collins said on Tuesday it may be appropriate to tighten policy soon, and she specifically noted the AI build-out appears to be putting upward pressure on core goods inflation - which ties the two halves of this brief together rather neatly.

Two live cautions and one date. Crude fell a fourth session for Brent and a fifth for WTI, to roughly $86.48 and $80.83 on the Reuters oil desk, because Qatar's Prime Minister travels to Tehran TODAY to relaunch Hormuz mediation. Cheaper oil is genuine disinflation arriving from diplomacy rather than from Washington, but it is reversible by a single incident - a tanker was struck by a projectile near Khasab, Oman, inside the same overnight window, and Treasury's promised designation of a large foreign financial institution still has NOT happened with Bessent's stated deadline landing this week. I will also flag a data disagreement honestly rather than paper over it: TradingEconomics had crude UP and about $1.80 higher this morning, against two separate Reuters snapshots showing it down, so we shipped the wire and logged the other feed as degraded. The date that matters is tomorrow at 10:00, when Chair Warsh gives his first Jackson Hole address; the symposium agenda does not even publish until 8:00 tonight. For clients: last night was a reminder that the AI complex is now priced off forward narrative rather than delivered results, and the semiconductor index still sits 20.7% below its own June record even after a 106% revenue quarter from its largest member - which is precisely why we size positions to a plan rather than to a print.

geo_headlines: THE NVIDIA PRINT IS THE MORNING, BUT THE TRADEABLE DETAIL IS THE 40 MINUTES IT SPENT DOWN: revenue $96.221B, +106% year over year, data-centre revenue $89.0B, +117%, non-GAAP EPS $2.22, and a Q3 guide of $108B plus or minus 2% against roughly $104.19B on LSEG consensus - all from NVIDIA's own release. The stock nonetheless opened the after-hours session LOWER. Reuters is the only account that reconciles the tape: shares were little changed for about 40 minutes, the mood picked up with the conference call, and Nvidia then rose 4.2% on more than 50 million shares. The catalyst inside those 40 minutes was forward-looking, not backward - roughly 70% revenue growth guided for fiscal 2028. Pre-market Thursday spans $223.62 to $225.21, up 6.7% to 7.4%. Two comparability caveats for the record: beginning fiscal Q1 2027 the non-GAAP measures NO LONGER exclude stock-based compensation, so $2.22 is not comparable to older non-GAAP series, and the $108B guide assumes ZERO China data-centre compute revenue, making it an ex-China floor.

THE MARGIN IS THE STORY THE HEADLINE BURIED, AND TWO COMPANIES NAMED THE IDENTICAL CAUSE: Nvidia guided gross margin DOWN - 74.0% plus or minus 50bp this quarter, troughing at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter and 72% to 73% for fiscal 2028, on rising memory costs. On the same evening HP Inc. beat revenue by $1.24B, raised its full-year EPS guide, and fell between 8.3% and 10.6% after its CFO flagged below-seasonal Q4 revenue on commodity-driven price increases and rising memory costs, with non-GAAP operating margin contracting to 6.5% from 7.1% and Personal Systems unit shipments DOWN 16% while revenue rose on price alone. When the largest AI winner and a mainstream PC maker independently blame the same input cost, that is a hardware cost cycle turning rather than a demand break - and it is a more durable fact than any single revenue beat. Boston Fed's Susan Collins made the macro connection explicit on Tuesday: the AI build-out appears to be putting upward pressure on core goods inflation.

HIKE ODDS ROSE AT EVERY SINGLE MEETING OVERNIGHT AND THE CUT PROBABILITY IS STILL EXACTLY ZERO: our CME cohort refreshed to Wednesday's settle and cumulative hike probability rose from 37.9% to 39.6% for September, 51.6% to 54.3% for October, 69.0% to 73.5% for December and 74.0% to 78.2% for January 2027 - verified field by field against yesterday's raw payload rather than against a summary. December now carries a 28.3% chance of TWO OR MORE hikes. The cause was yesterday's data. Core PCE held at 3.3% year over year, the 65th consecutive month above the 2% target per Reuters, with the unrounded monthly figure at 0.246%, just under the rounding boundary; supercore services ran +0.3% monthly and +3.9% annually. Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid: while July core PCE inflation came in line with consensus, the details of the release were more inflationary. Note honestly that even the in-line-versus-hot characterisation forked - CNBC called core in line against a Dow Jones 3.3% consensus while Morningstar called it stronger than expected against FactSet's 3.2%.

THE GDP REPORT CONTAINED THE MOST HAWKISH NUMBER NOBODY LED WITH: second-quarter real GDP was UNREVISED at +1.5% annualised, which reads soft. Underneath it, the price data was revised UP - the PCE price index to 5.3%, core to 3.6%, both 0.2 points higher than the advance estimate, and gross domestic purchases prices to 5.8% - while real final sales to private domestic purchasers came in at +4.2%, the STRONGEST IN OVER THREE YEARS, and consumer spending was revised up to 3.4% from 3.2%. Real gross domestic income was +2.2%, averaging 1.8% with GDP. Soft headline growth masking hot private domestic demand and firmer prices is close to the worst possible mix for a committee already 65 months above target. July durable goods reinforced the split: headline +1.1% to $339.3B beat the +0.5% expected, but core capital goods orders rose only +0.2% against +0.9% expected and ex-transport rose +0.4% against +0.6% - the beat was transportation, the capex core missed.

CRUDE FELL AGAIN ON DIPLOMACY THAT HAS NOT ACTUALLY HAPPENED YET, AND OUR TWO PRICE FEEDS DISAGREED: Brent fell a fourth consecutive session to $86.48, -1.55%, and WTI a fifth to $80.83, -1.70%, on the Reuters oil desk at 08:00 GMT, with the named cause being Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani travelling to Tehran TODAY to relaunch mediation over the Strait of Hormuz. Two pieces of counter-evidence sit inside the same window. UKMTO Warning 121-26 was issued around 00:54 GMT after a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile near Khasab, Oman. And Treasury Secretary Bessent's promised designation of a LARGE FOREIGN FINANCIAL INSTITUTION - he said Monday to expect it by the end of this week - has still NOT happened, which is a dated, asymmetric tail against the reopening consensus. Disclosed rather than smoothed: TradingEconomics showed Brent UP 0.50% at 88.278 and WTI unchanged at 82.22, roughly $1.80 above the wire on both. Both feeds reconstruct to the SAME prior settle, so the base agrees and the live print does not. Two independent Reuters snapshots beat one CFD feed; TE oil is logged DEGRADED.

JACKSON HOLE OPENS TODAY AND ALMOST NOTHING ABOUT IT IS PUBLIC YET - TREAT ANY AGENDA DETAIL THIS MORNING AS UNSOURCED: the Kansas City Fed's own release states verbatim that the full agenda will be available at kansascityfed.org on Thursday, Aug. 27, at 8:00 p.m. EDT, and that Chairman Kevin Warsh's remarks stream Friday, Aug. 28, at 10:00 a.m. EDT. The theme is Financial Innovation, Implications for Payments and Policy. Several third-party outlets reported a Wednesday-evening agenda drop and were wrong; an X post claiming a 19:30 Warsh slot is unreliable. There is NO Fed speaker at all today on the Board's own calendar. Reuters frames the stakes two ways worth quoting to clients: few investors expect Warsh to honour the tradition of a framework speech in his debut, and bond-market anxiety raises the stakes for it. Friday at 10:00 also collides with Michigan final sentiment, the BLS preliminary payroll benchmark revision and Q1 QCEW - all at the same minute. The September FOMC is 19 days out.

THE GUIDANCE-PUNISHMENT PATTERN IS NOW FOUR SESSIONS OLD AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO TELL A CLIENT THIS WEEK: of four large after-close reporters last night, THREE BEAT and TWO WERE SOLD. Salesforce beat with revenue $11.345B, +11%, lifted its full-year EPS guide to $16.67-16.71 from $14.06-14.12, and rose 11% to 13.9% - though note its GAAP EPS of $4.29 included a $2.6B investment gain largely from its Anthropic stake, so the EPS beat is not operating. CrowdStrike beat on revenue, earnings and free cash flow, raised both guides, and rose about 9.4% to $207.00. Synopsys grew revenue 42.4% to $2.477B, beat on EPS at $3.91 against $3.67, raised its full-year guide - and FELL 1.26%. HP beat by $1.24B and fell up to 10.6%. Wedbush's Matt Bryson made the point pre-print and it aged well: Nvidia has consistently exceeded consensus over the last three quarters yet the stock is roughly unchanged from October of last year. Marvell reports tonight at 4:45 into exactly this tape.

CENTRAL BANKS ARE TURNING HAWKISH IN PARALLEL, NOT JUST IN WASHINGTON, AND THE OVERNIGHT INDEX TAPE SHOWS IT: the Bank of Korea HIKED to 3.00%, a second consecutive increase, and the KOSPI still closed +1.53% at 6,912.37 after opening +2.76% and giving back more than half the gain. Australia's ASX 200 fell about 1% on a hotter-than-expected inflation print that raised RBA hike risk. That makes at least three developed central banks - the Fed, the BoK and the RBA - with the market leaning toward tightening rather than easing, which is a different world from the one most 2026 outlooks were written for. Elsewhere: Hang Seng -0.34% at 25,566, Shanghai Composite up between +0.24% and +1.13% depending on source with Xinhua at +1.13%, SENSEX -0.25%. Europe opened mixed - DAX +0.2% on Siemens Energy and SAP, AEX +0.55% on ASML and ASMI, FTSE 100 -0.5% on oil majors and miners, CAC 40 -0.41% on luxury, STOXX 600 -0.07% with the European tech sub-index +1.3%. The Nikkei is OMITTED for a second straight session: sources disagree on the SIGN.
